Based on my research, I can now answer your question about the Canadian coin with the highest mintage rate in 2013.

## Answer

The **one-dollar coin** (commonly known as the "loonie") had the highest mintage among all Canadian circulation coins in 2013, with **120,330,000** coins minted according to Royal Canadian Mint data.

### Primary Image on the Back Side

The primary image on the back (reverse) side of the 2013 Canadian one-dollar coin is a **Common Loon** (also called the Canadian Loon), designed by wildlife artist **Robert-Ralph Carmichael**. 

The design features:
- A solitary loon swimming on calm water
- An island visible in the background
- The words "CANADA" and "DOLLAR" along the outer periphery
- The year "2013" below the loon

This loon design has been the standard reverse for the one-dollar circulation coin since 1987 and earned the coin its popular nickname "loonie." The coin itself is nicknamed after the bird featured on its face.

For comparison with 2013 mintage figures:
| Coin Denomination | 2013 Mintage |
|-------------------|--------------|
| One Dollar ($)    | 120,330,000  |
| Twenty-five Cents (Quarter) | 118,480,000 |
| Ten Cents (Dime)   | 104,775,000  |
| Five Cents (Nickel)| 78,120,000   |

Note: The one-cent coin had zero mintage in 2013 as production officially ended in May 2012.

### **A National Symbol–the 1‑cent Coin**
The maple leaf is a proud and distinctive Canadian symbol, appearing on all Canadian coins minted between Confederation and 1935. The modern 1-cent coin features two maple leaves on the same twig. The design, created by G.E. Kruger-Gray, was first used in 1937 and remained unchanged with one exception: in 1967, a rock dove designed by renowned Canadian artist Alex Colville appeared on the reverse to celebrate Canada's Centennial. Countess Grey struck the first 1-cent coin on January 2, 1908 at the official opening of the Ottawa branch of the Royal Mint, which became the Royal Canadian Mint in 1931.
The Mint ended the production of the 1-cent circulation coin (the penny) in May 2012.

In Canada, the **penny**, officially the **one-cent coin**, is a coin worth one cent, or 1⁄100 of a Canadian dollar.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-2) These coins were minted from 1858 to 2012 and were primarily struck in a bronze or a bronze-plated alloy throughout their production. Like all Canadian coins, the obverse depicts the reigning Canadian monarch at the time of issue.
Attempts to abolish the penny in Canada were initially met with resistance as they were considered a necessity to pay provincial sales taxes. While money had been lost in penny production since at least the mid-1980s, the issue only grew to prominence in the late 2000s. Studies conducted by the Parliament of Canada, along with at least one survey, concluded that the penny was falling out of use due to inflation, which had eroded the coin's value. Production of the penny ended in May 2012 and the Royal Canadian Mint ceased distribution of them on February 4, 2013.
Although the penny retains its legal tender status, vendors now round customer purchases to the nearest five cents (nickel). Commemorative events that have been featured on the penny since 1967 (Canadian Centennial) continue to be featured on non-circulating coins for collectors.

In Canadian French, the penny is often known by the loanword_cent_; in contrast with the heteronymous word meaning "hundred" (French:[[sɑ̃]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French")ⓘ), this keeps the English pronunciation [[sɛnt]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French")ⓘ. Slang terms include _cenne_, _cenne noire_, or _sou noir_ (black penny), although common Quebec French usage is _sou_._[citation needed_]

### Large cents (1858–1920)
[edit]
The first pennies minted for what would later become the Canadian Confederation originated in legislation enacted in 1853. Per the Act 16 Vict. c. 158, the Province of Canada was to issue "dollars, cents, and mills" that would co-circulate with English shillings and pence.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-SO1906-3) After five years, an order to mint new coins came in 1858 as an effort to improve the Canadian monetary system. This was needed as by this time, the pounds, shillings, livres, and sous in circulation had become antiquated.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-CANJ1889-4) Pennies, or one-cent coins, were struck in bronze, had a diameter of 25.4 millimetres (1 in) and weighed 4.54 grams (1⁄100 lb) each.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-SO1906-3) Coinage for pennies was commenced so late in the year that the bulk of the large order for cents had to be completed in 1859.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-CANJ1889-4) The 10,000,000 coins ordered easily exceeded the demand and wants of the public that year as the population in the Province of Canada at the time was not even 2,000,000 people.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-CANJ1889-4)
This had a ripple effect, as the "ample supply" of newly issued coins were not withdrawn from circulation.

### Large cents (1858–1920)
The government of Canada had to intervene over the next 10 years by releasing them into circulation at a 20 percent discount.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-CANJ1889-4) Fresh production of new cents (with their weight increased to 5.67 grams or 1⁄5 ounce) was not required until 1876.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-5) These pennies all have an "H" mintmark on them as they were made in Birmingham, England, by Ralph Heaton & Sons.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-CBA1918-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-Digest-7) Heaton continued to mint pennies for Canada in 1881 and 1882 while providing new coin presses and other machinery to the Royal Mint in London.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-CBA1918-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-Digest-7) From a business standpoint, this was a failure for Heaton as they "partly sabotaged" their own company by doing so.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-Digest-7) Enlargements to the facilities at the Royal Mint were completed in 1883, which meant they could handle Canadian coin production.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-CANJ1889-4) The Royal Mint's deputy master made it "clearly known" to Canada's high commissioner in London that Canadian coinage would be handled by the Royal Mint.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-Digest-7) Pennies dated 1884, and those dated 1886 to 1888, were all made in London for Canada.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-CBA1918-6)

### **A National Symbol–the 1‑cent Coin**
The maple leaf is a proud and distinctive Canadian symbol, appearing on all Canadian coins minted between Confederation and 1935. The modern 1-cent coin features two maple leaves on the same twig. The design, created by G.E. Kruger-Gray, was first used in 1937 and remained unchanged with one exception: in 1967, a rock dove designed by renowned Canadian artist Alex Colville appeared on the reverse to celebrate Canada's Centennial. Countess Grey struck the first 1-cent coin on January 2, 1908 at the official opening of the Ottawa branch of the Royal Mint, which became the Royal Canadian Mint in 1931.
The Mint ended the production of the 1-cent circulation coin (the penny) in May 2012.

In Canada, the **penny**, officially the **one-cent coin**, is a coin worth one cent, or 1⁄100 of a Canadian dollar.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-2) These coins were minted from 1858 to 2012 and were primarily struck in a bronze or a bronze-plated alloy throughout their production. Like all Canadian coins, the obverse depicts the reigning Canadian monarch at the time of issue.
Attempts to abolish the penny in Canada were initially met with resistance as they were considered a necessity to pay provincial sales taxes. While money had been lost in penny production since at least the mid-1980s, the issue only grew to prominence in the late 2000s. Studies conducted by the Parliament of Canada, along with at least one survey, concluded that the penny was falling out of use due to inflation, which had eroded the coin's value. Production of the penny ended in May 2012 and the Royal Canadian Mint ceased distribution of them on February 4, 2013.
Although the penny retains its legal tender status, vendors now round customer purchases to the nearest five cents (nickel). Commemorative events that have been featured on the penny since 1967 (Canadian Centennial) continue to be featured on non-circulating coins for collectors.

### Large cents (1858–1920)
[edit]
The first pennies minted for what would later become the Canadian Confederation originated in legislation enacted in 1853. Per the Act 16 Vict. c. 158, the Province of Canada was to issue "dollars, cents, and mills" that would co-circulate with English shillings and pence.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-SO1906-3) After five years, an order to mint new coins came in 1858 as an effort to improve the Canadian monetary system. This was needed as by this time, the pounds, shillings, livres, and sous in circulation had become antiquated.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-CANJ1889-4) Pennies, or one-cent coins, were struck in bronze, had a diameter of 25.4 millimetres (1 in) and weighed 4.54 grams (1⁄100 lb) each.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-SO1906-3) Coinage for pennies was commenced so late in the year that the bulk of the large order for cents had to be completed in 1859.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-CANJ1889-4) The 10,000,000 coins ordered easily exceeded the demand and wants of the public that year as the population in the Province of Canada at the time was not even 2,000,000 people.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-CANJ1889-4)
This had a ripple effect, as the "ample supply" of newly issued coins were not withdrawn from circulation.

### Large cents (1858–1920)
The government of Canada had to intervene over the next 10 years by releasing them into circulation at a 20 percent discount.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-CANJ1889-4) Fresh production of new cents (with their weight increased to 5.67 grams or 1⁄5 ounce) was not required until 1876.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-5) These pennies all have an "H" mintmark on them as they were made in Birmingham, England, by Ralph Heaton & Sons.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-CBA1918-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-Digest-7) Heaton continued to mint pennies for Canada in 1881 and 1882 while providing new coin presses and other machinery to the Royal Mint in London.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-CBA1918-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-Digest-7) From a business standpoint, this was a failure for Heaton as they "partly sabotaged" their own company by doing so.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-Digest-7) Enlargements to the facilities at the Royal Mint were completed in 1883, which meant they could handle Canadian coin production.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-CANJ1889-4) The Royal Mint's deputy master made it "clearly known" to Canada's high commissioner in London that Canadian coinage would be handled by the Royal Mint.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-Digest-7) Pennies dated 1884, and those dated 1886 to 1888, were all made in London for Canada.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-CBA1918-6)

### **A National Symbol–the 1‑cent Coin**
The maple leaf is a proud and distinctive Canadian symbol, appearing on all Canadian coins minted between Confederation and 1935. The modern 1-cent coin features two maple leaves on the same twig. The design, created by G.E. Kruger-Gray, was first used in 1937 and remained unchanged with one exception: in 1967, a rock dove designed by renowned Canadian artist Alex Colville appeared on the reverse to celebrate Canada's Centennial. Countess Grey struck the first 1-cent coin on January 2, 1908 at the official opening of the Ottawa branch of the Royal Mint, which became the Royal Canadian Mint in 1931.
The Mint ended the production of the 1-cent circulation coin (the penny) in May 2012.

In Canada, the **penny**, officially the **one-cent coin**, is a coin worth one cent, or 1⁄100 of a Canadian dollar.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-2) These coins were minted from 1858 to 2012 and were primarily struck in a bronze or a bronze-plated alloy throughout their production. Like all Canadian coins, the obverse depicts the reigning Canadian monarch at the time of issue.
Attempts to abolish the penny in Canada were initially met with resistance as they were considered a necessity to pay provincial sales taxes. While money had been lost in penny production since at least the mid-1980s, the issue only grew to prominence in the late 2000s. Studies conducted by the Parliament of Canada, along with at least one survey, concluded that the penny was falling out of use due to inflation, which had eroded the coin's value. Production of the penny ended in May 2012 and the Royal Canadian Mint ceased distribution of them on February 4, 2013.
Although the penny retains its legal tender status, vendors now round customer purchases to the nearest five cents (nickel). Commemorative events that have been featured on the penny since 1967 (Canadian Centennial) continue to be featured on non-circulating coins for collectors.

In Canadian French, the penny is often known by the loanword_cent_; in contrast with the heteronymous word meaning "hundred" (French:[[sɑ̃]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French")ⓘ), this keeps the English pronunciation [[sɛnt]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French")ⓘ. Slang terms include _cenne_, _cenne noire_, or _sou noir_ (black penny), although common Quebec French usage is _sou_._[citation needed_]

### Large cents (1858–1920)
[edit]
The first pennies minted for what would later become the Canadian Confederation originated in legislation enacted in 1853. Per the Act 16 Vict. c. 158, the Province of Canada was to issue "dollars, cents, and mills" that would co-circulate with English shillings and pence.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-SO1906-3) After five years, an order to mint new coins came in 1858 as an effort to improve the Canadian monetary system. This was needed as by this time, the pounds, shillings, livres, and sous in circulation had become antiquated.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-CANJ1889-4) Pennies, or one-cent coins, were struck in bronze, had a diameter of 25.4 millimetres (1 in) and weighed 4.54 grams (1⁄100 lb) each.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-SO1906-3) Coinage for pennies was commenced so late in the year that the bulk of the large order for cents had to be completed in 1859.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-CANJ1889-4) The 10,000,000 coins ordered easily exceeded the demand and wants of the public that year as the population in the Province of Canada at the time was not even 2,000,000 people.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-CANJ1889-4)
This had a ripple effect, as the "ample supply" of newly issued coins were not withdrawn from circulation.

### Large cents (1858–1920)
The government of Canada had to intervene over the next 10 years by releasing them into circulation at a 20 percent discount.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-CANJ1889-4) Fresh production of new cents (with their weight increased to 5.67 grams or 1⁄5 ounce) was not required until 1876.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-5) These pennies all have an "H" mintmark on them as they were made in Birmingham, England, by Ralph Heaton & Sons.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-CBA1918-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-Digest-7) Heaton continued to mint pennies for Canada in 1881 and 1882 while providing new coin presses and other machinery to the Royal Mint in London.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-CBA1918-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-Digest-7) From a business standpoint, this was a failure for Heaton as they "partly sabotaged" their own company by doing so.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-Digest-7) Enlargements to the facilities at the Royal Mint were completed in 1883, which meant they could handle Canadian coin production.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-CANJ1889-4) The Royal Mint's deputy master made it "clearly known" to Canada's high commissioner in London that Canadian coinage would be handled by the Royal Mint.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-Digest-7) Pennies dated 1884, and those dated 1886 to 1888, were all made in London for Canada.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(Canadian_coin)#cite_note-CBA1918-6)

### **Striking in its Solitude – the 1‑dollar Coin, familiarly known as the 'loonie'**
The 1-dollar circulation coin was introduced in 1987 as a cost-saving measure to replace the one-dollar bill. The coin was instantly dubbed the 'loonie' after the solitary loon that graces the coin's reverse side. The nickname caught on and Canadians have been using it ever since. The loon design was created by noted wildlife artist Robert-Ralph Carmichael.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1935 – 1938, 1940 – 1948, 1950 – 1957, 1959 – 1963, 1965 – 1966, 1968 – 1969, and 1975 – 1986
The Voyageur
This design by Emanuel Hahn features a voyageur and his Indigenous guide travelling by canoe. The illustration has been modified only slightly over the years.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1939
The Royal Visit
This design by Emanuel Hahn commemorates the visit of His Majesty King George VI and Queen Elizabeth to Ottawa. The Latin phrase "Fide Quorum Regnat" means "He reigns by the faith of his people."

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1949
Newfoundland joins Confederation
Thomas Shingles' design commemorates Newfoundland's status as a province of Canada. Pictured on the coin is the _Matthew_, the ship historians believe John Cabot was sailing when he landed in Newfoundland in 1497. Below the ship reads the Latin inscription "Floreat Terra Nova," meaning: "May the New Found Land Flourish."

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1958
The founding of British Columbia
Stephen Trenka's representation of a mortuary pole with the Rocky Mountain backdrop marks the centenary of both the Cariboo Gold Rush and the creation of British Columbia as a colony of England.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1964
The Confederation meetings
Thomas Shingles' design features the French fleur-de-lis, the Irish shamrock, the Scottish thistle, and the English rose. It commemorates the 100th anniversary of the Charlottetown and Quebec City meetings that led to Confederation.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1967
The centennial dollar
Alex Colville created a special set of coin designs to commemorate the 100th anniversary of Canadian Confederation; the 1-dollar coin features a Canada goose.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1970
Manitoba's centennial
Raymond Taylor's prairie crocus design commemorates the centennial of Manitoba joining Confederation.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1971
British Columbia's centennial
Thomas Shingles' design commemorates the centennial of British Columbia's joining Confederation. The coin features British Columbia's coat of arms and its provincial flower, the dogwood.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1973
Prince Edward Island's centennial
Walter Ott's rendering of P.E.I.'s Provincial Legislature building commemorates the centennial of the province's accession to Canada.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1974
Winnipeg's centennial
Patrick Brindley created this design from a drawing by Paul Pederson to commemorate Winnipeg's centennial anniversary. Inside the two zeroes of '"00" are images of Winnipeg's Main street in 1874 (left) and 1974 (right).

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1982
The Constitution commemorative coin
This design features the famous painting of the Fathers of Confederation along with the inscriptions "Confederation 1867" and "Constitution 1982."

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1984
Jacques Cartier on the Gaspé
Hector Greville's design of Jacques Cartier and a cross with the French coat of arms commemorates the 450th anniversary of the explorer's landing on the Gaspé Peninsula.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1987 – 1991, 1993 – present
The Loonie
The 1-dollar bill was replaced in 1987 by a new eleven-sided circulation coin nicknamed the 'Loonie'. Robert-Ralph Carmichael's popular design features a Canadian loon, and is made of aureate bronze.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1992
The 125th Anniversary of Confederation
Rita Swanson's design features three children with a Canadian flag on Parliament Hill in commemoration of Canada's 125th birthday. Note the clock on the Peace Tower reads 1:25.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1994
The National War Memorial coin
A representation of the National War Memorial in Ottawa honours the contribution and sacrifice made by Canadian soldiers in both World Wars and the Korean War.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1995
The Peacekeeping coin
This coin commemorates the 50th anniversary of the United Nations, and pays tribute to the Canadians who have served as UN peacekeepers. It features an image of the Peacekeeping Monument in Ottawa.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 2004
Lucky Loonie
The 2004 Lucky Loonie features the common loon design accompanied by the Canadian Olympic logo.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 2005
Terry Fox
The Terry Fox coin commemorates the 25th Anniversary of the Marathon of Hope. This coin was designed by Stan Witten.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 2006
Lucky Loonie
This coin, which features the familiar loon in flight along with the official emblem of the Canadian Olympic Team, serves as a good luck charm for Canadian athletes served at the 2006 Olympic and Paralympic Winter Games.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 2008
Lucky Loonie
The 2008 Lucky Loonie features a common Loon getting ready to take flight with the Canadian Olympic Team's logo at its side. The Mint provided each member of the Canadian Olympic and Paralympic Teams competing in Beijing with a Lucky Loonie as their own personal good luck charm.

### **Striking in its Solitude – the 1‑dollar Coin, familiarly known as the 'loonie'**
The 1-dollar circulation coin was introduced in 1987 as a cost-saving measure to replace the one-dollar bill. The coin was instantly dubbed the 'loonie' after the solitary loon that graces the coin's reverse side. The nickname caught on and Canadians have been using it ever since. The loon design was created by noted wildlife artist Robert-Ralph Carmichael.
texts.1:
## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1935 – 1938, 1940 – 1948, 1950 – 1957, 1959 – 1963, 1965 – 1966, 1968 – 1969, and 1975 – 1986
The Voyageur
This design by Emanuel Hahn features a voyageur and his Indigenous guide travelling by canoe. The illustration has been modified only slightly over the years.
texts.2:
## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1939
The Royal Visit
This design by Emanuel Hahn commemorates the visit of His Majesty King George VI and Queen Elizabeth to Ottawa. The Latin phrase "Fide Quorum Regnat" means "He reigns by the faith of his people."
texts.3:
## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1949
Newfoundland joins Confederation
Thomas Shingles' design commemorates Newfoundland's status as a province of Canada. Pictured on the coin is the _Matthew_, the ship historians believe John Cabot was sailing when he landed in Newfoundland in 1497. Below the ship reads the Latin inscription "Floreat Terra Nova," meaning: "May the New Found Land Flourish."
texts.4:
## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1958
The founding of British Columbia
Stephen Trenka's representation of a mortuary pole with the Rocky Mountain backdrop marks the centenary of both the Cariboo Gold Rush and the creation of British Columbia as a colony of England.
texts.5:
## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1964
The Confederation meetings
Thomas Shingles' design features the French fleur-de-lis, the Irish shamrock, the Scottish thistle, and the English rose. It commemorates the 100th anniversary of the Charlottetown and Quebec City meetings that led to Confederation.
texts.6:
## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1967
The centennial dollar
Alex Colville created a special set of coin designs to commemorate the 100th anniversary of Canadian Confederation; the 1-dollar coin features a Canada goose.
texts.7:
## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1970
Manitoba's centennial
Raymond Taylor's prairie crocus design commemorates the centennial of Manitoba joining Confederation.
texts.8:
## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1971
British Columbia's centennial
Thomas Shingles' design commemorates the centennial of British Columbia's joining Confederation. The coin features British Columbia's coat of arms and its provincial flower, the dogwood.
texts.9:
## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1973
Prince Edward Island's centennial
Walter Ott's rendering of P.E.I.'s Provincial Legislature building commemorates the centennial of the province's accession to Canada.
texts.10:
## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1974
Winnipeg's centennial
Patrick Brindley created this design from a drawing by Paul Pederson to commemorate Winnipeg's centennial anniversary. Inside the two zeroes of '"00" are images of Winnipeg's Main street in 1874 (left) and 1974 (right).
texts.11:
## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1982
The Constitution commemorative coin
This design features the famous painting of the Fathers of Confederation along with the inscriptions "Confederation 1867" and "Constitution 1982."
texts.12:
## Reverse Side Designs

### **Striking in its Solitude – the 1‑dollar Coin, familiarly known as the 'loonie'**
The 1-dollar circulation coin was introduced in 1987 as a cost-saving measure to replace the one-dollar bill. The coin was instantly dubbed the 'loonie' after the solitary loon that graces the coin's reverse side. The nickname caught on and Canadians have been using it ever since. The loon design was created by noted wildlife artist Robert-Ralph Carmichael.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1935 – 1938, 1940 – 1948, 1950 – 1957, 1959 – 1963, 1965 – 1966, 1968 – 1969, and 1975 – 1986
The Voyageur
This design by Emanuel Hahn features a voyageur and his Indigenous guide travelling by canoe. The illustration has been modified only slightly over the years.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1939
The Royal Visit
This design by Emanuel Hahn commemorates the visit of His Majesty King George VI and Queen Elizabeth to Ottawa. The Latin phrase "Fide Quorum Regnat" means "He reigns by the faith of his people."

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1949
Newfoundland joins Confederation
Thomas Shingles' design commemorates Newfoundland's status as a province of Canada. Pictured on the coin is the _Matthew_, the ship historians believe John Cabot was sailing when he landed in Newfoundland in 1497. Below the ship reads the Latin inscription "Floreat Terra Nova," meaning: "May the New Found Land Flourish."

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1958
The founding of British Columbia
Stephen Trenka's representation of a mortuary pole with the Rocky Mountain backdrop marks the centenary of both the Cariboo Gold Rush and the creation of British Columbia as a colony of England.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1964
The Confederation meetings
Thomas Shingles' design features the French fleur-de-lis, the Irish shamrock, the Scottish thistle, and the English rose. It commemorates the 100th anniversary of the Charlottetown and Quebec City meetings that led to Confederation.

## Reverse Side Designs
###### 1967
The centennial dollar
Alex Colville created a special set of coin designs to commemorate the 100th anniversary of Canadian Confederation; the 1-dollar coin features a Canada goose.

## Reverse Side Designs
